statement: On 17 June 1972, five men were arrested inside Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex while attempting to repair surveillance equipment installed during an earlier entry.
timeBasis: Date stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: The source is an official retrospective history, not a contemporaneous arrest record.

statement: While the burglars awaited arraignment, the FBI opened an investigation and press reporting raised questions and suggested connections between Nixon's reelection campaign and the defendants.
locator: Origins, account of the initial investigation and reporting
notes: This records the existence of an investigation and reported questions; it does not adopt every press allegation or establish White House knowledge.

statement: On 30 August 1972, President Nixon announced that John Dean had investigated the matter and found no involvement by White House personnel.
timeBasis: Date stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: Recorded as a contemporaneous public explanation, not as an established finding.

statement: Seven men were indicted on 15 September 1972 for their roles in the June break-in; five pleaded guilty and two were convicted in January 1973.
timeBasis: First date in the claim; source supplies dates but no UTC times.

statement: The Senate created the Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities on 7 February 1973 to investigate the 1972 election campaign and related conduct.
locator: Creation and mandate of the committee
timeBasis: Date stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.

statement: In public Senate testimony, former White House counsel John Dean alleged that President Nixon approved plans to conceal White House involvement in the break-in.
notes: This is testimony and was an allegation when given; later documentary evidence is represented separately.

statement: On 16 July 1973, Alexander Butterfield testified that President Nixon had installed a voice-activated system that automatically recorded Oval Office conversations.
notes: The testimony established the existence of a recording system; it did not establish the content of any tape.

statement: On 23 July 1973, the Senate committee and Special Prosecutor Cox subpoenaed White House tapes and documents; President Nixon refused to comply with Cox's subpoena on 25 July.
timeBasis: Date the subpoenas were issued; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: Records the subpoena and refusal without resolving the legal dispute.

statement: On 20 October 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson refused the President's order to dismiss special prosecutor Archibald Cox and resigned; Acting Attorney General Robert Bork then dismissed Cox.
timeBasis: Date stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: Commonly called the Saturday Night Massacre.

statement: The White House disclosed that one subpoenaed conversation contained an approximately 18.5-minute gap; the available official chronology does not establish who caused the erasure or why.
timeBasis: Date of disclosure stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: The gap is established; attribution and intent are not asserted.

statement: White House Tape 741-2 records a 23 June 1972 Oval Office conversation between President Nixon and H. R. Haldeman, six days after the arrests.
timeBasis: Nixon Library gives 10:04 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time; converted to UTC (UTC-4).
notes: Archival audio and description are primary evidence; electronic transcripts may differ from the recording.

statement: The Nixon Library's description of Conversation 741-2 says Nixon and Haldeman discussed the FBI's tracing of Watergate money and a proposal that CIA officials ask the FBI to halt that line of investigation on national-security grounds.
timeBasis: Conversation start converted from 10:04 a.m. EDT to UTC.
notes: The claim paraphrases the official archive description and does not rely on an unofficial transcript.

statement: On 1 March 1974, a federal grand jury indicted seven former presidential aides and named the President as an unindicted co-conspirator in sealed materials considered in United States v. Nixon.
locator: 418 U.S. at 687 n.2 and procedural history
timeBasis: Date stated in the opinion; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: An indictment and grand-jury designation are not a conviction of the President.

statement: The Watergate Road Map was a grand-jury report consisting of a two-page summary, 53 numbered statements, and 97 supporting documents transmitted under seal to the House Judiciary Committee.
locator: NARA description, Grand Jury Report and Recommendation
timeBasis: Date the report was delivered under seal; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: The Road Map organized evidence for Congress; it was not itself a trial verdict.

statement: The special prosecutor obtained a subpoena for tape recordings and documents relating to meetings between the President and persons indicted by the grand jury; the President moved to quash the subpoena.

The Supreme Court unanimously held that a generalized interest in confidentiality did not justify an absolute presidential privilege against a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.
timeBasis: Decision date; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: The Court recognized a presumptive confidentiality interest but rejected an absolute privilege in this context.

statement: The Supreme Court affirmed enforcement of the subpoena and remanded for in-camera review and appropriate handling of the subpoenaed material.
timeBasis: Decision date; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.

statement: The House Judiciary Committee's first proposed article of impeachment found that the President and his agents pursued a course of conduct designed to delay, impede, and obstruct investigation of the Watergate entry and to conceal those responsible.
timeBasis: Date Article I was adopted by committee; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: A committee finding and proposed impeachment article, not a full-House vote or criminal conviction.

statement: Article I identified means including false or misleading statements, withholding evidence, influencing witnesses, payments to obtain silence, misuse of the CIA, and interference with investigative bodies.
notes: These are the Judiciary Committee majority's charged means.

statement: The Judiciary Committee adopted a second article alleging abuse of presidential powers and a third article alleging failure to comply with committee subpoenas.
locator: H. Rept. 93-1305, Articles II and III, pp. 23761-23764
timeBasis: Date Article III was adopted; Article II was adopted 29 July; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: Committee action only; the full House did not vote on the articles.

statement: The committee report includes separate, supplemental, dissenting, and minority views, preserving disagreement over the evidence, legal standards, and proposed articles.
locator: H. Rept. 93-1305, table of contents and pp. 23828-23872
notes: The dataset does not treat the committee report as unanimous.

statement: On 9 August 1974, Richard Nixon resigned the office of President of the United States by letter to the Secretary of State.
excerpt: I hereby resign the Office of President of the United States.
timeBasis: Effective date stated in the letter; no UTC time in the document.
notes: The full House and Senate therefore did not complete an impeachment trial process.

statement: On 8 September 1974, President Ford granted Richard Nixon a full, free, and absolute pardon for federal offenses he had committed or may have committed during his presidency.
timeBasis: Proclamation date; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: The pardon foreclosed a federal criminal adjudication of the former President's conduct covered by the grant.

statement: Congress enacted the Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act in 1974, placing Nixon presidential materials in federal custody and requiring priority processing of materials relating to Watergate and abuses of power.
locator: Prologue article, section on the 1974 preservation act
timeBasis: Enactment date identified by NARA; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.
notes: This is later institutional action preserving the evidentiary record.

statement: The constitutional record demonstrates that courts can adjudicate a subpoena dispute involving a President and that a qualified confidentiality interest can yield to the needs of criminal justice.
notes: Analytical inference limited to the holding and justiciability analysis of United States v. Nixon.

statement: The August 1972 public assurance of no White House involvement conflicts with later-recorded evidence and the Judiciary Committee majority's cover-up findings.
locator: H. Rept. 93-1305, Article I and statement of information concerning presidential knowledge
notes: Analytical comparison of W-C003 with W-C012 and W-C018; it does not assert what every White House employee knew in August 1972.

statement: Nixon released transcripts in April 1974 while withholding the recordings themselves; the dispute over the recordings continued until the Supreme Court decision and compliance with the subpoena.
timeBasis: Date transcripts were publicly released; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.

statement: The House authorized its Judiciary Committee on 6 February 1974 to investigate whether sufficient grounds existed to impeach President Nixon.
timeBasis: Date stated by source; midnight UTC is a date-only placeholder.

statement: The historical record represented here does not establish a completed impeachment judgment or criminal verdict against President Nixon because he resigned and was later pardoned.
locator: Watergate and the Constitution, constitutional process overview
notes: This limitation prevents committee findings, grand-jury materials, and tape evidence from being mislabeled as a conviction.

statement: A responsible presentation should preserve event dates and source posture so that testimony and allegations are not silently converted into facts established only by later recordings, judicial rulings, or committee findings.
locator: Watergate and the Constitution, teaching-document framework
notes: Analyst recommendation derived from the sequence and differing authority of the official sources; not a historical finding.
